title: Buddy Rich puts him on the map
summary: He played trumpet in Buddy Rich's band for about four months, learned much, and then wrote for it because Rich respected his players as writers.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: How do you — what was your entrance like into that world?

Well Buddy Rich of course put me on the map. You know I played trumpet on Buddy’s band for about four months. He fired me a couple of times, at least a couple of times. But I learned a lot on that band. Of course playing in bands, like with my parents with our family band, you understand how things work. You hear the melody then you hear the counter line. And when I was playing in college, when I played in big bands in college, I had my own big band in Potsdam. Well you get to hear all those inner voicings and inner workings. And that’s why single line instrumentalists make the best arrangers. Piano players and guitar players are the hardest people to teach. But a single line instrument — let me put it this way — a non-breathing player, a non-breathing instrument player has the hardest time writing, because they don’t have to breathe. But a horn player or a wind player, put it that way, are the people who really get it quickly. You know like Billy Byers and Slide Hampton, we can go right down — Bill Holman, go right down on the list. But I forgot where we were going with this.
Well I wondered how you, like if there was a real door that opened you, for your composing and I think you said Buddy Rich because you came back and started writing for him, is that correct?

Yes. I enjoyed the band. You know he respected me and if he respected you he would take a chance on you — if he respected you as a player he’d take a chance on you as a writer. That’s why a lot of the guys in the band were writing charts for the band, because he respected their playing and he would listen to what they had to write. Well I was on the Glenn Miller band for three years, almost three years with Buddy DeFranco. And I learned a lot from him as well. So all the time I was on the Glenn Miller band I was writing arrangements, I was transcribing the Miller stuff off the 78 recordings, because a lot of that music disappeared. The real arrangements disappeared. And a lot — I mean we had the library in New York City which I’d go through, all the Bill Finegan stuff, but a lot of times I was transcribing from a 78 recording on a cassette tape in the back of the bus. Anyway, so I made all my mistakes on the Glenn Miller band. And then we were in England on tour and I said I can’t do this. Because I looked across the aisle at an alto player named, oh God, why can’t I think of his name, it’ll come back to me. He’d been on the band with every road band there was, Al Thompson. He was a second alto player. He played in every band and that’s all he did. He was an alcoholic and I looked across and I said that could be me, you know, at the end of my life just sitting there on the damn band bus, you know, playing one-nighters. So I gave my notice in England and I was back in Rochester on unemployment. A lot of people helped us out like for instance Vince Falcone who was Frank Sinatra’s accompanist. He ran a piano company, the Shale Piano Company in Rochester. And he would give us the pianos the people traded in. He gave Chuck Mangione one, he gave Pat one, he gave me one.
